strengths: Addresses a fundamental limitation of current amortised Bayesian inference (ABI) methods—namely, rigidity to fixed priors and the inability to cleanly perform sequential Bayesian filtering without retraining or unbounded context growth.

The proposed architecture is conceptually clean and well-motivated: treating Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) components as unordered sequence tokens processed by a permutation-equivariant transformer decoder, with observations incorporated via cross-attention.
Maintains approximate conjugacy (mapping GMM priors to GMM posteriors), which uniquely enables recursive filtering where posterior tokens can directly serve as the prior tokens for subsequent steps.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning analytical conjugate benchmarks, GP predictive posterior inference with hyperpriors, quantum parameter inference, and non-linear sequential tracking/stochastic volatility tasks.

Thorough supplementary analyses in the appendix, including scaling with latent dimensionality up to 24D, meta-prior misspecification, ablation of the prior loss term, GMM component count transfer, and sequential error accumulation across 100 timesteps.
weaknesses: The exact mechanism of the sequential state-transition update (the prediction step) between timesteps in Section 4.3 and Appendix I/J needs further clarification. It is not entirely explicit in the main text whether the system dynamics are propagated analytically through the GMM prior before being fed into the DT update, or if the DT itself models the transition-plus-update jointly.

Scalability to higher-dimensional latent spaces: Parameterizing full covariance matrices per GMM token incurs an $\mathcal{O}(D^2)$ parameter footprint per component. While the 24D experiment in Appendix C.1 is encouraging, many Bayesian inverse problems feature hundreds of latent dimensions, where full covariances become prohibitive without low-rank or diagonal structural approximations.

In the sequential filtering experiments (Section 4.3), baselines are restricted to classical non-amortised algorithms (EKF, Particle Filter). Comparing against, or discussing, amortised recurrent/autoregressive neural filters (e.g., recurrent state-space models or sliding-window transformer filters) would provide a clearer benchmark against neural sequential estimation baselines.

strengths: Conceptual Elegance and Originality: The idea of treating probability distributions as permutation-invariant sequences of GMM tokens processed via transformer decoders is both elegant and natural. Exploiting permutation equivariance in transformers to match the symmetry of mixture components provides a principled bridge between amortised Bayesian inference (ABI) and recursive Bayesian filtering.

Addresses a Major Limitation in ABI: Existing amortised frameworks (e.g., PFNs, TabPFN) are predominantly restricted to fixed training priors and cannot be recursively composed due to output distribution mismatches. Distribution Transformers achieve flexible, on-the-fly prior conditioning and approximate conjugacy within the GMM family.

Comprehensive Empirical Evaluation: The method is validated across a diverse spectrum of benchmarks, including analytical conjugate settings, GP hyperparameter inference, quantum parameter estimation, and challenging non-linear/non-Gaussian sequential filtering (e.g., stochastic volatility and sensor fusion), consistently demonstrating competitive log-likelihoods and orders-of-magnitude speedups over classical sampling/VI baselines.

Thorough Ablation Studies: The appendix provides extensive and insightful analyses addressing key practical questions: latent dimensionality scaling up to 24 dimensions, out-of-distribution meta-prior robustness, inference-time generalization across GMM component counts, the regularizing impact of the prior loss, and multi-step error accumulation over sequential horizons.
weaknesses: Scalability Bottlenecks in Latent Dimension: Because each token decodes full covariance matrices, parameter and memory costs scale quadratically with the dimension of the latent variable ($O(D^2)$ per component). While the paper demonstrates success up to 10D and 24D, scaling to very high-dimensional Bayesian problems (e.g., high-dimensional field inversion or deep generative latents) remains a significant challenge without diagonal or low-rank covariance parameterizations.

Sensitivity and Reliance on Meta-Prior Design: The inference quality depends heavily on the coverage and quality of the meta-prior $p(\phi)$ used during the offline simulation/training phase. Although Appendix C.2 tests a shifted inverse-gamma distribution, broader out-of-distribution meta-prior evaluation across diverse parametric families remains limited.

Algorithmic Clarification on Sequential Predict Steps: In the sequential inference experiments (Section 4.3), while the update step via cross-attention is well-detailed, the exact implementation of the dynamical prediction step—specifically whether propagation through non-linear/linear dynamics is performed analytically on the GMM components or mapped in latent space—could be articulated with greater mathematical and algorithmic precision in the main text.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated framework: The paper tackles a key bottleneck in amortised Bayesian inference (ABI)—namely, the inability of standard amortised models (e.g., PFNs) to adapt to changing priors at test time and to perform recursive filtering due to a lack of closure under Bayesian updates.

Architectural elegance: Treating continuous densities as permutation-invariant Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) tokens in a transformer decoder naturally leverages self-attention for intra-distribution component interactions and cross-attention for data conditioning, providing an intuitive formulation of approximate conjugacy.

Breadth of empirical evaluation: The evaluation covers a diverse suite of benchmarks, spanning analytical verification (tractable conjugate problems), intractable posterior inference (GP hyperpriors and quantum parameter estimation), and sequential Bayesian filtering (non-linear sensor fusion and 10-dimensional stochastic volatility).

Strong empirical performance and runtime: Across static and sequential experiments, the proposed method matches or outperforms existing amortised baselines (PFN, TabPFN, ACE) and classical sampling/optimization approaches (SVI, PF, EKF) in terms of log-likelihood and KL divergence, while retaining amortised inference speeds.

Comprehensive supplementary analysis: The appendix provides valuable analyses addressing potential practitioner concerns, including scaling behavior up to 24 dimensions, meta-prior distribution shifts, component count generalisation, and error propagation over sequential steps up to depth 100.
weaknesses: Lack of clarity on the dynamic prediction step in sequential filtering: In Section 4.3 and Appendices I–J, it is not sufficiently explicit how the state propagation (time-update/prediction step) is handled between filtering steps. While GMMs propagate in closed form under linear-Gaussian transition dynamics, non-linear dynamics generally break GMM closure; clarifying the exact division of labor between analytic propagation and DT inference is critical for reproducibility.

Embedding of non-GMM priors breaks symmetry: For GMM priors, component-wise permutation invariance is preserved naturally, but for general parametric priors (Appendix D), the paper relies on distinct, non-shared MLPs branching from a single parameter vector to generate the k latent tokens. This breaks the exchangeability of components prior to the self-attention blocks and restricts flexibility to pre-specified parametric families.

Scalability limitations in high latent dimensions: Parametrizing full covariance matrices via Cholesky factors scales quadratically with latent dimension D (O(k * D^2) parameters per token). While the synthetic ablation in Appendix C.1 explores latent dimensions up to D=24, practical high-dimensional Bayesian inverse problems common in simulation-based inference (SBI) remain beyond reach without diagonal or low-rank covariance constraints.

Baseline conditioning disparities: Baseline models such as standard PFNs were evaluated by marginalizing over the meta-prior, inherently handicapping them in wide-prior regimes where prior knowledge varies heavily. Meanwhile, TabPFNv2 is an off-the-shelf tabular classification/regression model rather than a tailor-trained continuous parameter inference network.
